It was a privilege to join thousands of shipbuilders, Navy leaders and personnel, local residents, and supporters at Bath Iron Works today for the christening of the future USS William Charette (DDG-130). This Bath-built ship is named in honor of Medal of Honor recipient Master Chief Hospital Corpsman William Charette. During the Korean War, Charette shielded a wounded Marine from an enemy grenade with his own body. Despite suffering facial wounds and shock from the blast, he improvised bandages from his clothing and continued treating wounded Marines under enemy fire. His actions were directly responsible for saving many lives. Through this ship, his courage, humility, and devotion to others will continue to inspire generations of sailors.

Today, the Senate HELP Committee voted to advance bipartisan legislation I introduced with Senators Tim Kaine and Lisa Murkowski to prevent the Department of Education from transferring critical offices responsible for special education and rehabilitative services, postsecondary education, elementary and secondary education, and Indian education to other federal agencies that lack the staff and expertise needed to execute their missions. One of the offices protected by our bill manages programs established under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, known as IDEA, that help meet the educational needs of more than 8 million children with disabilities. Moving this work to the Department of Health and Human Services fundamentally misunderstands the purpose of the Special Education program. It is focused primarily on students’ educational needs, not their health care needs. Every American, regardless of background or disability, deserves access to a quality public education. These important landmark programs must remain at the Department of Education, where Congress specifically placed them and where they belong.

B000490.text: This week, the White House Office of Budget and Management’s Director, Russell Vought, appeared before the U.S. House Appropriations Subcommittee on Financial Services and General Government. During the hearing, I asked the Director about how Congress can be any clearer to ensure that the Trump Administration understands that once a funding bill is signed into law, the President is not allowed to change or second-guess the spending and withhold it due to policy or political differences. That is at the heart of Article 1 of the U.S. Constitution and why Congress also passed the Impoundment Control Act of 1974, when President Nixon tried to withhold funds that were already obligated according to the law.

This week, I asked the White House Office of Budget and Management’s Director, Russell Vought, to explain how poorly planned cuts to the federal workforce last year have weakened services and protections upon which Americans rely. This includes the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, which is responsible for protecting America’s agriculture from invasive species and diseases. USDA-APHIS began mounting a vigorous response to the resurgence of New World Screwworm – a deadly parasite affecting livestock – in 2024. However, in early 2025, the Administration illegally fired workers and forced others to resign, causing over 25 percent of all USDA-APHIS employees to leave. USDA’s New World Screwworm prevention, monitoring, surveillance, and control efforts were halted. USDA had approved $378 million in prevention and control funding for sterile fly facilities in 2023 and 2024, yet the money went unspent when the new administration paused funding. This is extremely concerning to our ranchers, and this outbreak could drive the price of food even higher. Unfortunately, we continue to see the fallout of the blunt and ill-considered cuts to federal workers, from the return of New World Screwworm to the United States, to farmers showing up to closed or understaffed Farm Service Agency offices, to attacks on our nuclear safety programs putting national security at risk. I will continue to hold the White House accountable, as I did this week during the U.S. House Appropriations Subcommittee on Financial Services and General Government hearing with Mr. Vought.

C001053.text: It is with heartfelt sadness that I learned of the passing of my dear friend, and magnificent former colleague, Kay Granger of Fort Worth, Texas. Some simply hold the gavel – Kay demonstrated what it meant to wield it. Her life and career were defined by a remarkable legacy of firsts: the first woman to become Mayor of Fort Worth, the first Republican woman elected to Congress from Texas, the first woman to Chair the Appropriations Defense Subcommittee, and the first woman to lead House Republicans on the Appropriations Committee. Yet, Kay never rested in the remarkableness of each milestone – she was always ready for the next responsibility, the next challenge, and the next opportunity to serve. I admired Kay Granger the moment I met her. She carried herself with an unmistakable grace, but behind her regal appearance was a razor-sharp tenacity that commanded any room. Kay demanded respect, and she got it from everyone she ever interacted with. Whip-smart and Texas tough, she had a presence that could settle any debate with little more than a look. I was lucky enough to know her personally and professionally through our work serving together in Republican leadership. So, I can attest with firsthand knowledge that ‘Don’t mess with Texas’ was more than a motto when it came to Kay. I know it well because I lost to her when we both sought the chairmanship of the Appropriations Committee previously. After that, our friendship and mutual respect didn’t change for one another. In fact, she named me to be her Vice Chair. Her mentorship and guidance were large parts of my own committee journey and helped prepare me for the privilege of succeeding her as Chairman. On the Appropriations Committee, Kay was known as a fiscal conservative, a defense hawk, and a hard – but fair – negotiator. Ever proud of her Texas roots, Granger ferociously fought for the interests of the Lone Star State. Her colleagues on both sides of the aisle always respected her professionalism, her good humor, her unfailing civility, and her willingness to strike a deal. Indeed, she and the first woman to Chair the Appropriations Committee, Nita Lowey of New York, were fast friends. They were partners who set the gold standard of how to achieve bipartisan consensus. Their portraits above our dais today remind us of the example they set and the responsibility we inherit. I will miss my friend Kay Granger. She set an unmatched standard of excellence, civility, professionalism, and dedication to duty that few can match – and no one will ever exceed. My thoughts and prayers are with Kay’s family, friends, and many admirers. We have lost a great lioness of the House, and I have lost a dear friend to whom I shall always be indebted.

It takes dedication and principle. And it takes the resounding belief that upholding those ideals and values is worth the fight because America is bigger than any one person. Because liberty can only truly endure when it is paired with responsibility, virtue, and a commitment to put public good ahead of personal ambition. Today, we celebrate the moment when our founding fathers openly declared that creating this country, based in liberty, was a necessity in the face of tyranny. Their legacy is that leadership requires courage when it’s difficult, integrity when no one is watching, and a willingness to put country above self. We must remember that our duty is not merely to the next election, but to the next generation. That should be the challenge for all Americans as we look forward to another 250 years. From Massachusetts, where the fight for freedom first began, I wish you a happy 4th of July. God Bless America always, God Bless all who call her home, and God Bless our courageous men and women in uniform who continue the fight for liberty today.

On Monday, our office suffered an unimaginable loss. Chris Matthews, my District Outreach and Communications Director, passed away unexpectedly. If any one of you begin to lose faith in our country, remember Chris Matthews. Remember he was without question one of the Commonwealth’s sharpest political minds – a generational talent. Remember that he was more than a Congressional aide. He took the belief that through our actions we all can bring needed change and brought it with him on many interstate bus rides to canvas distant pivotal states and to the doors of the families he inspired. Remember through his example that public service is a genuinely noble vocation. As a trusted member of our office, he helped countless veterans, families, and those who could not advocate for themselves. Those of us privileged to have worked with him for over fifteen years will remember his laugh and his wry, often biting, humor – contrasting the way things are to the way they could be. We will always remember his authentic belief that in this country, people can bring about progress and meaningful change. It was real to him and his sincerity shown through. Chris was a genuinely good person. He was family to all of us, and we are devastated by his loss, particularly at such a young age. Our thoughts and prayers are with Molly and Eli and the many who loved him. Though we wish we had more time with him, his memory will continue to give us faith that one person can significantly make better the lives of those around him.

I enjoyed visiting Keaton Cattle Company and meeting with Freddie, Renee, and their daughter, Kinley Keaton, to discuss the opportunities and challenges facing Missouri’s cattle producers. Freddie not only operates an impressive cattle operation, but also serves as President of the Independent Cattlemen of Missouri and R-CALF Region VI Director, where he is a strong voice for independent producers. We had a great conversation about the need for fairer markets, increasing competition in the cattle industry, reforms to mandatory price reporting to improve transparency and price discovery, ensuring family ranchers have the opportunity to compete—not just the Big Four meatpackers—and the importance of tackling emerging animal health threats like Theileria that are impacting cattle producers across our state. I appreciated hearing how the Working Families Tax Cuts are already helping Freddie invest in the future of his operation. He’s planning to build a new commodity barn to better store feed for his cattle, and thanks to immediate expensing, he’ll be able to deduct that investment right away, making it easier to reinvest in his farm. Families like the Keatons are the backbone of rural Missouri. I’ll continue fighting for policies that strengthen independent producers, expand market opportunities, support animal health research, reduce burdens on family farms, and help ensure the next generation can continue Missouri’s proud cattle tradition.

Only eight command staff members in the history of the Middletown Township Police Department had ever graduated from the FBI National Academy. Last month, Lieutenant Aileen Parker, this week’s Hometown Hero, became the ninth. That is an extraordinary accomplishment, and one that reflects the officer, leader, and public servant she has proven herself to be throughout her career. As a former FBI Special Agent, I know the standard the FBI National Academy represents within law enforcement. Quantico is where proven officers and command leaders are challenged at the highest level — in judgment, discipline, communication, physical fitness, command presence, character, and the responsibility of leading the men and women who protect our families, neighborhoods, schools, and businesses. Lieutenant Parker earned her place there, and she brings that standard of excellence home to Middletown Township. But this achievement is not the sum of her career. It is a reflection of it. At MTPD, Lieutenant Parker has played a major role in the critically important, often unseen work that makes police departments strong: supervision, operations, training, accreditation, accountability, professional standards, officer development, and the daily leadership required to support officers and protect the community. She has continued to raise the standard at every level— completing the FBI-LEEDA Trilogy and graduating from Northwestern University’s School of Police Staff and Command, where she was selected by her peers to serve as class president and deliver the keynote address. Those achievements reflect what her colleagues already know: Lieutenant Parker leads with preparation, credibility, discipline, and earned respect. Strong communities need strong law enforcement. And strong law enforcement depends on leaders who keep learning, keep improving, keep supporting their officers, and keep bringing excellence back home. Lieutenant Parker is one of those leaders. Please join me in congratulating Lieutenant Aileen Parker on this outstanding achievement and thanking her for her service to Middletown Township. Here in PA-1, we are blessed to have some of the finest law enforcement officers anywhere in America. Let us come together to continue to thank them, support them, stand with them, and never take for granted the incredible men and women who put on the uniform, answer the call, and protect our families, neighborhoods, schools, businesses, and communities every single day.

When duplicative inspections and outdated federal requirements drive landlords out of affordable housing programs, families pay the price: fewer available homes, fewer choices, and longer waits for a place they can afford. Across our community, where limited supply and rising costs are already putting housing out of reach for too many families, these barriers were making an urgent challenge even worse. The Choice in Affordable Housing Act was one of the central initiatives I led as part our bipartisan Affordability Agenda. Signed into law earlier this month, this bill will modernize the Housing Choice Voucher program, strengthen landlord participation, and give more of our PA-1 families access to safe, affordable homes. This law is progress, but not the finish line. We will keep cutting barriers, expanding supply, and lowering housing costs across our community and nationwide.

Affordability is about whether families can put down roots, businesses can grow, and communities can thrive. My work with our local families, business owners, and community organizations helped shape the priorities I brought to the Problem Solvers Caucus, where colleagues from both side of the aisle came together to build our Bipartisan Affordability Agenda. Earlier this month, four bills from that agenda were signed into law—a major step forward, and momentum we are determined to build on. Thank you to the Cato Institute and Ryan Bourne for such a great conversation about what comes next, and how we continue turning affordability solutions shaped by the people and communities we serve into bipartisan law.

Fun Fact Friday: As we celebrate the 250th anniversary of American independence, I want to highlight some of the signers of the Declaration of Independence. Richard Henry Lee was born in Virginia in 1732. At age 16, he sailed to England to continue his education. While he was studying in England, his parents died, leaving him an orphan. Returning to the colonies, Lee volunteered to raise a military company for the French and Indian War. In 1758, he was elected to the House of Burgesses. Seeking to serve his community, Lee applied to be a tax collector during the Stamp Act period. This led him to be censured and began his support for the cause for independence. While serving in the Second Continental Congress, he drafted what was known as the Lee Resolution that was used as guidance for the Declaration of Independence. He signed the Declaration in August of 1776.

L000571.text: RT by @SenLummis: @leereiners - Not sure if your post counts as a subtweet, exactly, but I wouldn’t have minded your tagging me. As you know, I’m a firm believer in a robust debate on these important issues, and I have always valued your perspective, even when we disagree – sometime strongly. The fact here is that your premise is foundationally mistaken. It is Judge Rakoff’s decision that was the outlier and, regardless, referring to a handful of federal cases, almost all of which were decided at a motion to dismiss - the most preliminary stage – as “most of crypto’s history” is uncharacteristically misleading on your part. The fact is that the federal case law that exists on this topic remains unsettled, but it had unquestionably been trending away from the position you advocate (for example, you failed to mention Judge Orrick’s key decision in Payward, which affirmatively admonishes the SEC for referring to tokens as “crypto asset securities”). As I wrote about extensively in Ineluctable Modality (which reviewed and indexed every single federal appellate Howey case), courts have consistently taken a flexible view when a purported sale of a product or service appears in economic reality to be more appropriately considered a fundraising scheme subject to the federal securities laws. That’s right on policy and right on law. However, the position you advocate for in your article is not that, nor is it what is contained in the Clarity Act July text. Howey-type fundraising would remain subject to the federal securities laws and places measured obligations on the fundraising party. (It is fair to ask whether those obligations are too measured, but “Reg Crypto” and most of the features you describe were the subject of a multi-year policy discussion and relatively little has changed in that regard since the January 2026 text.) The consistent problem you face, and the fundamental flaw of the position you advocate for, is that most tokens are simply not themselves securities in any cognizable way. That is, unlike any other type of financial instrument recognized as a security, if you examined a given token on its face, assuming it did not provide “disqualifying financial rights”, you would not be able to identify it as a “security”. Critically most tokens lack the fundamental element of a security - a security’s “ineluctable modality“ if you will - an issuer who, if dissolved and no longer in existence, would mean that the security also no longer exists. That is the case for every other security that has ever existed. Why is that so essential? Because a security is not the paper, or token, or other means of conveyance, of rights. The security is the inchoate rights themselves, the *legal relationship* that directly binds a holder to an identifiable issuer. Those rights do not need to be embodied in a formal contract (and as many reading this know, I have disagreed with those suggesting that). An investment scheme subject to the federal securities laws can be created with the wink of an eye, the nudge of an elbow, or any set of actions that reasonably create the four Howey elements. You and I have discussed this and you know that I agree that many fundraising schemes involving tokens fall neatly within the parameters of our federal security laws. The problem arises when two third parties deal in something (like a token) that is not itself a security, but has “security-ness” artificially imputed on it in order to achieve a separate policy objective. The persons or entities exchanging that asset have no way of determining with certainty whether or not they are engaged in regulated transaction. This violates fundamental due process and is also essentially unworkable. (Continues in comments)

I stopped by Branhilda Richardson Knowles Memorial Park in Deerfield Beach to pay respect to an important piece of our local history. I was proud to help secure funding for this park when I was a state legislator.   Born in the Bahamas, Branhilda Richardson Knowles came to Deerfield Beach in 1922 and served as a midwife for the African American community at a time when segregation denied many Black residents access to hospitals and other medical care.   The park that now bears her name also preserves a historic African American cemetery, where Black and Bahamian residents were buried during the Jim Crow era because they were prohibited from being laid to rest in the city cemetery.   Grateful to see how Deerfield Beach has worked to honor the people who helped build the community we know today.

On this day in history in 1492, Christopher Columbus and his crew set sail for China and India on the Niña, Pinta, and Santa Maria. The crew returned to Spain with gold and spices. Columbus would make four expeditions to the Americas over the course of his lifetime. Columbus died in 1506 never realizing he founded the New World for Europe, which would help make Spain the wealthiest country on Earth for a century.

M001228.text: RT by @RepMaloyUtah: On Pioneer Day, I had the opportunity to tour Beaver and see firsthand the devastating impact of both wildfire and flooding. Standing in those burned and flooded landscapes, talking with the Forest Service personnel, local leaders, and the people of Beaver one thing was crystal clear: forest management works. The difference between treated and untreated forest was visible. Areas that had been thinned or otherwise managed gave firefighters a chance. They slowed the fire, reduced its intensity, helped crews establish containment lines, and in some cases, stopped the fire altogether. In the overgrown, untreated areas, the fire burned hotter, moved faster, and left behind far greater destruction, burning an unprecedented 70,000 acres in two days. It's frustrating that while the United States is the world's largest importer of lumber and paper products, millions of acres of our own forests sit overcrowded and vulnerable to catastrophic wildfire. The boots-on-the-ground Forest Service personnel managing these forests know what needs to be done and want to actively manage these lands, but too often commonsense projects are delayed or stopped by endless litigation and opposition by environmentalists and bureaucrats in Washington D.C. That's why the Fix Our Forests Act deserves to move forward. The legislation passed the House with strong bipartisan support, but has been stalled in the Senate for 18 months. It needs to move forward. I'm grateful to Congresswoman Celeste Maloy for bringing us together to see this firsthand, and to the Trump Administration officials who came to Utah to witness these conditions on the ground. With the U.S. Forest Service headquarters coming to Utah, we have a tremendous opportunity to ensure the people making decisions about our forests are closer to the landscapes and communities they serve. Thank you to USDA's Michael Boren, Sam Crofts from the Bureau of Land Management, and Chairman Bruce Westerman of the House Natural Resources Committee for taking the time to be there and hear directly from those who have been impacted by this catastrophe. On Pioneer Day weekend, that lesson feels especially meaningful. The pioneers who settled this state understood that stewardship requires hard work, planning, and taking responsibility for the land we call home. We honor their legacy not by leaving our forests untouched until they burn and cause catastrophic damage, but by actively caring for them so they remain healthy for generations to come. The Beaver community continues to show incredible resilience. I was reminded why I'm so proud to be a Utahn. We face challenges head-on, we help our neighbors, and we don't shy away from doing the difficult work that's necessary to protect our communities and our public lands. @realDonaldTrump @RepMaloyUtah @RepWesterman @SenJohnCurtis @RepBurgessOwens @RepMikeKennedy @USDA @forestservice @Interior @BLMNational @NatResources @JStuartAdams @cralbrecht52 @BeaverCountyUT

S001201.text: ROAD TO 250: The Road to Independence On August 2, 1776, the Declaration of Independence was formally signed by the delegates of the Second Continental Congress. Although Congress voted for independence on July 2 and approved the Declaration's final text on July 4, the delegates gathered nearly a month later at the Pennsylvania State House—now Independence Hall—to sign the official parchment. Those signatures transformed a bold declaration into a solemn pledge. By putting their names to the document, 56 delegates accepted the risks of treason and affirmed their commitment to the new American republic. As we continue to mark America's 250th anniversary, we remember not only the words that declared our independence, but also the courage of the men who signed them.

ROAD TO 250: Long Island & Queens Legacies Jupiter Hammon's story is an important part of Long Island's history—and America's. Born into slavery in 1711 at the Lloyd Manor estate in present-day Lloyd Harbor, Hammon became the first published African American poet in the United States. A writer, preacher, and thinker, he used his words to explore faith, freedom, and the moral questions of his time. I previously had the opportunity to tour the historic Joseph Lloyd Manor, where Hammon lived and wrote for much of his life. It was a reminder that the Road to 250 is not just about our nation's best-known founders, but also about the people whose lives and contributions helped define America's story. As we continue our Road to 250, Hammon's life reminds us that the American story is enriched by voices that were too often overlooked, but whose contributions continue to shape our understanding of our nation's past.

Sixty-one years ago, President Lyndon B. Johnson signed bipartisan legislation establishing Medicare and Medicaid. Today, these two programs provide more than 150 million Americans—including seniors, children, families, and people with disabilities—with access to affordable health care, helping ensure their health, security, and dignity. As a Member of Congress, I will continue working across the aisle to protect and strengthen these vital programs. We should build on their success by ensuring Medicare and Medicaid remain strong, sustainable, and available for the Americans who rely on them today and for generations to come.

ROAD TO 250: Long Island & Queens Legacies Target Rock in Lloyd Harbor is more than a scenic landmark—it is a reminder of Long Island’s place in our nation’s history. The wildlife refuge takes its name from a 14-foot-tall glacial boulder standing just offshore in Huntington Bay. For generations, the rock served as a navigation marker for mariners and was reportedly used for cannon and target practice during both the Revolutionary War and the War of 1812. During the American Revolution, the British established "East Fort" nearby to help defend the harbor, and Lloyd Neck became home to Loyalists displaced by the conflict. As America approaches its 250th anniversary, places like Target Rock help tell the story of how the Revolutionary War shaped communities here on Long Island and across the nation.

By strengthening partnerships with NASA, our universities, our military installations, and the private sector, we can ensure Alaska remains a key player in space innovation.   I appreciate Administrator Isaacman taking the time to discuss our shared vision and look forward to working together to ensure Alaska continues to serve as a vital launch point for discovery and as a key component in our nation's space leadership strategy.

J000311.text: Today, I was honored to welcome Speaker of the Georgia House of Representatives Jon Burns to the University of West Georgia to discuss the legacy and leadership of the late Speaker Tom Murphy. As we celebrate our country’s 250th anniversary, I am proud to honor the memory of one of the greatest Georgians to ever come from our district: the longest-serving Speaker of the Georgia House of Representatives in our state’s history, Tom Murphy. Speaker Burns and I toured Speaker Murphy’s replica office preserved in the Ingram Library, and we had an insightful discussion with Speaker Murphy’s children, former aides, and legislators who previously served in the General Assembly with him. I was honored to welcome my friend, the Ambassador of Hungary to the United States, @_SzabolcsTakacs to Haralson County today. In the late 1800s, dozens of Hungarian families moved from Pennsylvania's coal mines to Haralson County to establish a wine-making community.  They named their village Budapest after the Hungarian capital, and planted vineyards across the surrounding hillsides.  After Prohibition was enacted in the 1920s, many of the families left, and all that remains from that era is a home which once served as a Catholic rectory and the historic Budapest cemetery.  Today, we visited both. Ambassador Takács' visit is a special moment in Haralson County's rich history, and I am grateful for the incredible support the Haralson County Historical Society, the Hungarian Community Church of Georgia, the Dogwood Hills team, and local officials and community leaders provided to facilitate this meaningful event. Thank you, Ambassador Takács, for visiting Georgia's 3rd Congressional District, and thank you for strengthening the relationship between Hungary and the United States of America! @HungaryinUSA

RT by @RepBrianJack: Grateful to join the amazing Steve Gradick of WLPP and @RepBrianJack in Carrollton, Georgia yesterday for a fun long chat on all things America, agriculture, and saving our country. We announced the finalized Cooperative Interstate Shipment (CIS) agreement, giving qualifying Georgia state-inspected meat processors the opportunity to ship USDA-labeled products across state lines. This is a tremendous victory for Georgia's farmers, ranchers, and small meat processors. Yesterday, Georgia became one of only a handful of states participating in the Cooperative Interstate Shipment Program—allowing qualifying state-inspected meat processors to ship USDA-labeled products nationwide. For too long, a handful of massive processors have dominated the market, putting family-owned processors at a disadvantage. This is another step toward expanding opportunity, strengthening rural America, increasing competition, and rebuilding America's food production capacity. Under Biden, the United States flipped from net agricultural exporter to net importer. Four years of weakness turned a historic American strength into a strategic vulnerability. We’re fixing that. Food security is national security. Thank you Georgia!!! 🥩🐂🇺🇸

WORLD_FRANCE_PRESIDENT.text: Face à la situation migratoire à Ceuta, j’ai été en contact avec le Président du gouvernement espagnol pour marquer notre solidarité et proposer toute aide nécessaire, y compris via Frontex. Je salue la coopération en cours avec le Maroc, qui a déjà permis aujourd’hui plus de 40 000 retours de Ceuta vers le Maroc. Les ministres de l’Intérieur sont en contact pour assurer un suivi étroit de la situation. Ceuta ne bénéficie pas de la libre circulation vers le reste de l’espace Schengen. J’ai toutefois demandé dès hier au Ministre de l’Intérieur de renforcer les contrôles à notre frontière avec l’Espagne si cela devait être nécessaire : 4 unités de forces mobiles, des avions et des drones sont déployés. Ces mesures viennent renforcer les dispositions que nous avons prises depuis 2020 pour mieux protéger notre frontière avec l’Espagne en étroite coordination, avec des brigades communes et une action conjointe de lutte contre l’immigration clandestine. Ces mesures viennent compléter les instruments européens adoptés pour assurer les retours et appliquer le pacte asile et migrations, avec 25% de chute des flux irréguliers vers l’Union européenne l’an dernier et une baisse poursuivie sur les routes migratoires atlantique et de Méditerranée occidentale en 2026. Solidarité et responsabilité avec nos partenaires européens pour faire appliquer nos règles de fermeté en matière de retours et de protection des frontières extérieures de l’Union. Je redis ici notre solidarité à l’Espagne, son gouvernement et son peuple.
